Both `main.py` and `readme` are empty, so there's no existing setup to follow — you're starting fresh. Here's how to set up a venv:

```bash
cd /Users/andrewxiao/Documents/projects/jobqueue
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # zsh/bash; use .venv/bin/activate.fish for fish
```

You have Python 3.14.2 available, so `python3 -m venv .venv` will use that.

Once activated, your prompt should show `(.venv)`, and `pip install <package>` will install into the venv instead of system Python. To install deps later from a `requirements.txt`:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-08-07 23:02:34Z)**_

No — venvs are a Python-specific concept (isolating Python packages). Go doesn't use them at all.

For Go, dependency isolation is handled per-module via `go.mod`/`go.sum`, not a virtual environment:

```bash
cd /Users/andrewxiao/Documents/projects/jobqueue
go mod init <module-name>   # e.g. github.com/yourname/jobqueue
```

That creates a `go.mod` file that pins your Go version and dependencies. Each project's deps live in its own `go.mod`, so there's no need for anything venv-like — the `go` toolchain and `GOPATH`/module cache handle isolation globally.

If this project is going to be Go rather than Python, want me to clean up the empty `main.py`/`readme` and scaffold a proper Go module instead?

A .proto file is a contract that describes two things: what data looks like, and what functions can be called between two services.

Think of it like this: you're writing a Go service, and someone else is writing a Python service. Normally, if Go code wants to call Python code (or vice versa), there's no direct way to do that — they're different languages, they don't understand each other's function calls or data types.

The .proto file solves that by being a language-neutral description of:

The data — "a MatchRequest has a candidate with skills, a location, and a comp range" (this is the message part)
The functions — "you can call ScoreMatches, send it a MatchRequest, and it sends back a MatchResponse" (this is the service/rpc part)

You write this description once, in one file, and then a tool called protoc reads it and generates real code in each language — Go code for your side, Python code for theirs. So both sides end up with matching, type-safe code that knows how to talk to each other, even though neither of you wrote the other's language.

Why you're making a test one first, instead of jumping straight to the real matching-engine proto:

You're currently learning three new things at once — proto syntax, the protoc code-generation step, and gRPC server/client wiring. If you try to learn all three and get your real business logic (skills matching, scoring) right at the same time, and something breaks, you won't know which of the four things went wrong.

The test proto strips it down to the simplest possible version — "send a name, get back a greeting" — so you can prove the mechanics work (proto compiles → generates Go code → server runs → client calls it → gets a response) without any real complexity in the way. Once that loop works end-to-end, you swap in your actual matching-engine data and logic, and you're only dealing with new problems (the real scoring logic), not re-debugging the plumbing.

It's the same reason you'd test "can I turn on this light switch" before wiring up a whole house — confirm the basic connection works, then build the real thing on top of a foundation you already trust.

ok so make the strucutre of the proto. the test is made then how does it hypothetically become the actual contract ?

Here's the test proto structure, then the path from "test works" to "this is now the real contract."

test.proto (recap):

protobuf
syntax = "proto3";

package test;

option go_package = "example.com/test/proto";

message HelloRequest {
  string name = 1;
}

message HelloResponse {
  string message = 1;
  int32 word_count = 2;
}

service Greeter {
  rpc SayHello(HelloRequest) returns (HelloResponse);
}

How this "becomes" the real contract — it's not automatic, you deliberately evolve it:

The test proto proves the mechanism works. The real matching.proto is a new file, structurally identical, but with your actual data instead of "name" and "greeting." You're not upgrading the test file in place — you're copying the pattern into a new one.

Step 1 — Swap the shape, keep the skeleton:

protobuf
syntax = "proto3";

package matching;

option go_package = "github.com/yourteam/matching-engine/proto";

message Candidate {
  repeated string skills = 1;
  string location = 2;
  int32 min_comp = 3;
}

message JobPosting {
  string id = 1;
  repeated string required_skills = 2;
  string location = 3;
}

message MatchRequest {
  Candidate candidate = 1;
  repeated JobPosting postings = 2;
}

message MatchResult {
  string posting_id = 1;
  float score = 2;
}

message MatchResponse {
  repeated MatchResult results = 1;
}

service MatchingEngine {
  rpc ScoreMatches(MatchRequest) returns (MatchResponse);
}

Same syntax, package, option go_package pattern, same message → service → rpc structure. Only the field names/types and the actual service name changed. This is why the test was worth doing — you already know exactly what each line does.

Step 2 — This becomes the actual shared contract:

You send this .proto file (or put it in a shared repo/folder) to Person B, who's building search-service in Python. They run protoc against the exact same file, but with Python output flags instead of Go ones:

bash
protoc --python_out=. --grpc_python_out=. matching.proto

Now you both have generated code — yours in Go, theirs in Python — from the same source of truth. Neither of you hand-writes network/serialization code; it's all generated from that one file.

Step 3 — Where it lives so both sides can rely on it:

Since two different repos (your Go service, their Python service) both need this exact same file, the practical answer is usually one of:

A shared proto/ repo both services pull from (cleanest, avoids drift)
Or, for a small 3-person project, just: whoever changes it pastes the updated file to the others and everyone regenerates.

Step 4 — Once it's "live," changes are no longer free:

This is the part that matters once it's the real contract instead of a test toy: you don't renumber or remove fields once someone else's code depends on them. If you need to change min_comp to something else, you add a new field with a new number, you don't repurpose = 3. That's the discipline that makes it a real contract instead of a moving target — it's exactly why you agreed on this shape with Person B early, per what I flagged earlier.

So the honest short answer to "how does test become real": you don't convert the file, you apply the pattern you now understand to a new file describing your real data, and that new file — shared with Person B and generated on both sides — is the contract.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-08-07 23:05:05Z)**_

Got it — here's the layout, no files touched:

```
jobqueue/
  test/
    proto/
      test.proto          # the HelloRequest/HelloResponse/Greeter contract
    go/
      go.mod               # go mod init for this test module
      go.sum
      proto/                # generated *_pb.go and *_grpc.pb.go land here
      server/
        main.go             # implements Greeter, listens on a port
      client/
        main.go             # dials the server, calls SayHello
```

Notes on the pieces:

- **`test/proto/test.proto`** — single source of truth, same content you already have above.
- **`test/go/`** — its own Go module (own `go.mod`), separate from the rest of the repo. `go_package` in the `.proto` should point at `test/go/proto` (or whatever module path you pick) so generated code lands in the right place.
- **`test/go/proto/`** — output of `protoc --go_out=. --go-grpc_out=. test.proto`, generated, not hand-written.
- **`server/main.go`** and **`client/main.go`** — separate binaries so you can run `go run ./server` in one terminal and `go run ./client` in another, proving the round trip works.

Later, the real thing mirrors this exactly: `matching-engine/proto/matching.proto`, `matching-engine/go/...`, swap `test`/`Greeter` for `matching`/`MatchingEngine`.
